cues.text: Let's turn now to release planning and dependencies, which is the third chapter of this study session.
Start with what release management actually is.
Release management plans, coordinates, validates, authorises, deploys and reviews changes.
Notice that this is a whole chain of activities, not just the moment of pushing software live.
And the purpose of all of it is to protect business continuity and quality.
In other words, the organisation should keep running, and the product should stay good, while change flows into it.
One important idea here is that a release may expose functionality separately from technical deployment.
The mechanism the source gives for this is feature flags.
So deploying code to a production environment and letting users see a feature can be two distinct decisions.
The code can be technically deployed, while the feature stays hidden until it is deliberately switched on.
Next, what should a release plan define?
The source lists these in order.
Objectives.
Scope and features.
Acceptance.
Version.
Schedule.
Dependencies.
Stakeholders.
Owners.
Test evidence.
Risk assessment.
Approvals.
Communication.
Migration.
Rollback and recovery.
Monitoring.
And support.

That is sixteen items, and together they answer questions such as: what are we releasing, why, when, who is involved, how do we know it is ready, and what do we do if it goes wrong, and how do we look after it afterwards.
Now consider who does what.
The release manager coordinates readiness.
The product owner prioritises value.
Engineering owns implementation.
QA verifies evidence.
And operations and security manage the applicable controls.
Each role has a distinct contribution, so readiness is a shared effort rather than one person's job.
To make those responsibilities unambiguous, we use RACI.
RACI clarifies four things: Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed.
The letters R, A, C and I stand for those four words, in that order.
It is a way of stating, for each activity, who does the work, who answers for it, who gives input, and who simply needs to be told.
Let us move on to versioning.
Semantic versioning uses the format MAJOR dot MINOR dot PATCH.
Each number has its own meaning, and the source gives them in order.
MAJOR signals incompatible API changes.
MINOR signals backwards-compatible functionality.
PATCH signals backwards-compatible fixes.
And this all operates under a declared public API.
That qualification matters: the meaning of "incompatible" or "compatible" is measured against the public API that the project has declared.
Then dependency management.
It includes versions and lockfiles, compatibility, an SBOM, review, and an upgrade plan.
SBOM stands for software bill of materials.
So you track which versions you depend on and pin them with lockfiles, you check that they are compatible, you keep an SBOM, you review dependencies, and you plan how to upgrade them.
Now databases, which are often the hardest part of a release.
Database migrations use a backward-compatible expand, migrate, contract approach where feasible.
Note the words "where feasible"; the source does not claim it is always possible.
The key requirement is that the old and new versions must safely coexist.
While a release is rolling out, both versions of the application may be running against the same data, so the database changes must not break either one.
Closely related is recovery.
Back up, and validate restore.
A backup is only useful if you have confirmed that you can restore from it.
And a crucial warning: rollback code may not undo data changes.
You can roll the application code back, but that does not automatically reverse changes already made to the data.
Finally, risk.
Document a risk register.
For each risk, record the likelihood and impact, an owner, a mitigation, a contingency, and the residual risk, which is the risk that remains afterwards.
And two firm rules close this chapter.
Risk acceptance must be authorised, so nobody can quietly decide to live with a risk.
And critical security and legal requirements cannot be bypassed for a deadline.
A schedule is never a valid reason to skip them.
